title: Garhwal on a budget: real costs for 2026
meta_description: Garhwal on a budget: UTC and GMOU bus fares, GMVN and dharamshala beds, food, ponies and permits, with daily costs from ₹1,800 and a sample 7-night plan.
summary: Garhwal is one of the cheapest parts of the Himalaya to travel in. A careful traveller using UTC and GMOU buses, shared jeeps, GMVN dorms, dharamshalas and dhaba thalis spends ₹1,800–3,000 a day. Ponies, helicopters and private cars are what blow budgets; plan around them and travel in late September or October.

sections.heading: What a day really costs
paras: We plan saver trips in Garhwal at ₹1,800–3,000 per person a day, excluding the train or bus to Rishikesh. That covers a bed in a dorm, dharamshala or shared room, two or three dhaba meals, and a share of the day's bus or jeep fare. It does not cover ponies, porters, helicopter seats, rafting or private taxis, which we treat as separate decisions.

The range is wide because the region is. Rishikesh has hostels, ashrams and cheap cafes, and a day there can cost ₹1,200. High on the yatra roads in May and June, when every room in Badrinath or Guptkashi is in demand, the same bed costs two or three times as much. The single biggest saving is timing: travel from the second half of September through October, when the monsoon has gone, the shrines are still open and hotel rates on the yatra road drop by a third or more.
The table below gives the costs we see on the ground. All are indicative for 2026, per person unless stated, and will move with fuel prices and season.

sections.heading: Getting around for less
paras: Buses are the backbone of budget travel here. Uttarakhand Transport Corporation (UTC) runs from the Rishikesh ISBT, and the private Garhwal Motor Owners' Union (GMOU) runs from its yard close by. Both send buses to Uttarkashi, Barkot, Sonprayag, Ukhimath, Joshimath and Badrinath between about 4 am and 7 am. In season, seats on the earliest buses sell out a day ahead, so book the evening before at the counter.

A bus seat from Rishikesh to Sonprayag costs ₹500–800; a private taxi for the same run costs ₹7,000–9,000. Even split four ways, the taxi costs three times as much per head. Where buses do not run, shared jeeps fill the gap: Joshimath to Govindghat or Badrinath, Uttarkashi to Harsil and Gangotri, Barkot to Janki Chatti. They leave when full, mostly in the morning, so plan to change vehicles before 1 pm.
A few rules keep bus travel safe and calm:
list: Never plan a bus or jeep journey after dark on hill roads; drivers avoid it and so should you.
Sit on the valley side if you get motion sick, and eat lightly before the ride.
Keep your Char Dham registration on your phone and as a printout; it is checked on the road.
Keep one spare day in every trip for landslides, especially in July and August.

sections.heading: Where to sleep cheaply
paras: Garhwal Mandal Vikas Nigam, the state tourism corporation known as GMVN, runs tourist rest houses along every yatra road, including Badrinath, Ghangaria, Gangotri, Uttarkashi and Joshimath. They are plain, usually clean, and have dorm beds as well as doubles. Book on GMVN's official site or at its Rishikesh office as soon as your dates are fixed; in May and June the cheapest beds go first.

Temple towns also have dharamshalas run by trusts, communities and the temple committees, where a bed or simple room costs ₹300–1,500. Facilities are basic and rules strict, with closing times, no alcohol and vegetarian food. The gurdwaras at Rishikesh, Govindghat and Ghangaria offer shelter and free langar to pilgrims of every faith; leave a donation if you can.

In Rishikesh, the cheapest comfortable beds are in hostels in Tapovan and around Lakshman Jhula, and ashrams such as Parmarth Niketan rent rooms to guests who follow their routine. In villages like Sari near Deoria Tal, and around Harsil, family homestays charge ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. That is not the cheapest bed, but the food is home-cooked and the money stays in the village.

sections.heading: Food, water and small costs
paras: Food is cheap if you eat where pilgrims eat. A thali of rice, dal, sabzi and roti costs ₹150–300 at dhabas on the yatra roads, and Maggi with tea is the walker's staple at every chatti. Langar at gurdwaras is free and open to everyone. Try local food where it is offered: mandua roti from finger millet, jhangora kheer from barnyard millet, and kafal berries sold by the roadside in May and June.

Prices rise with altitude because everything is carried up by road and then by mule. A bottle of water that costs ₹20 in Rishikesh can cost ₹40–60 on the Kedarnath path. Carry a steel bottle and fill it at the RO water points on the yatra routes; it saves money and plastic. Budget a little each day for tea, snacks, temple offerings and tips.

sections.heading: The big-ticket items to plan around
paras: Four things can double a budget trip. The first is ponies and palkis. On the Kedarnath path a pony costs ₹2,500–4,500 each way at notified rates; at Yamunotri ₹1,500–2,500; from Pulna to Ghangaria ₹1,500–3,000. Walk if you are fit and acclimatised, or use a pony for one direction only, usually the climb.

The second is helicopters. A return seat to Kedarnath costs about ₹6,000–13,000 plus GST, sold only on the IRCTC HeliYatra portal; any other seller is a scam risk. The third is private taxis, which save time but cost ₹4,000–5,000 a day. The fourth is peak dates: the opening week of the shrines, Ganga Dussehra in Haridwar, and the Christmas week in Mussoorie all raise room rates sharply. Check current status before you travel, because fares and rules change each season.

sections.heading: A sample 7-night saver budget
paras: Here is how our Valley of Flowers and Hemkund trip by bus adds up for one person on twin sharing in late July, starting and ending in Rishikesh. It costs about ₹18,500, and you can trim it further by sleeping in the gurdwara at Ghangaria and eating langar.

Most of the spend is beds, and the rest splits between food and transport. A Kedarnath and Badrinath trip by bus over the same number of nights costs about the same, plus whatever you spend on a pony or helicopter.

sections.heading: Money, ATMs and payments
paras: UPI works in most shops and dhabas in Rishikesh, Uttarkashi, Srinagar and Joshimath, but signal fails on high roads and treks, and payments can hang for minutes. Carry enough cash for two or three days at a time. Draw it in Rishikesh, Srinagar, Uttarkashi or Joshimath; ATMs above these towns run dry in peak weeks. Keep small notes for shared jeeps, porters and tea.

faqs.q: How much money do I need for a week in Garhwal?
faqs.a: On a saver plan, about ₹13,000–21,000 per person for 7 nights, plus travel to Rishikesh. That covers dorms or simple rooms, dhaba food and buses. Add ₹5,000–13,000 if you use a pony or helicopter to Kedarnath.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to do the Char Dham?
faqs.a: Use UTC and GMOU buses and shared jeeps, sleep in GMVN dorms and dharamshalas, walk the treks and travel in late September or October. A full Char Dham this way takes 10–12 days and costs roughly ₹25,000–35,000 per person.

faqs.q: What is the bus fare from Rishikesh to Kedarnath?
faqs.a: Buses go to Sonprayag, the road head, for about ₹500–800, taking 7–9 hours. A shuttle jeep to Gaurikund costs ₹50–100, and the last 16–17 km is on foot, pony or palki.

faqs.q: Are GMVN rest houses good value?
faqs.a: Yes, for budget travellers. They are plain but usually clean, have dorms and doubles, and sit in useful places on every yatra road. Book early for May and June on GMVN's official site.

faqs.q: Can I stay free at gurdwaras in Garhwal?
faqs.a: Gurdwaras at Rishikesh, Govindghat and Ghangaria offer shelter and free langar to pilgrims of any faith, especially on the Hemkund route. Space is shared and basic. Follow the rules, cover your head inside and leave a donation if you can.

faqs.q: When is Garhwal cheapest to visit?
faqs.a: Late September to October for the high valleys, when rates drop after the monsoon and the shrines are still open. Rishikesh and Mussoorie are cheapest on weekdays outside school holidays and the Christmas week.

faqs.q: Is UPI accepted in Badrinath and Kedarnath?
faqs.a: Many shops and lodges accept UPI, but signal is weak and payments fail in crowds or bad weather. Carry enough cash for two or three days and draw it in Rishikesh, Uttarkashi or Joshimath.

faqs.q: How much does a pony to Kedarnath cost?
faqs.a: About ₹2,500–4,500 one way at government-notified rates in recent seasons. Book only at the official counters in Sonprayag or Gaurikund and keep the receipt. Rates change, so check current status before you travel.
Yes. Hostel dorms cost ₹500–1,000, thalis ₹150–300 and drop-in yoga classes ₹300–700. Rafting costs ₹800–1,200. A frugal day there can be under ₹1,500.
